text: “New Zealand has spoken, but we’re not sure what they’ve said yet.” – Chris Hipkins (Labour Party leader)

Background of New Zealand election
Economic stress
Electoral reform and breakdown in electoral “norms”

What is the likely structure of government?
At face value the current government will return (National-ACT-NZF coalition). However:
Special votes tend to boost left-leaning parties.
Multiple cabinet members lost their seats (including Finance – which is the Treasurer equivalent).
NZF leader went on a podcast saying he wanted to join a coalition with Labour.
Currently, a left coalition would need at least five parties.
Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori (left block)
Opportunity (first timers)
New Zealand First (NZF) – if two electorates flip to Labour, they would not be needed.

What does this mean for policy
A reelected centre-right government means:
No capital-gains tax introduced.

Replacing KiwiSaver with compulsory superannuation.

No PBO.

Ministry of Regulation will not be shut – other departments likely to be cut further.

Electoral reform more likely to involve cutting electorates (especially Māori), rather than increasing the number of list seats.
